claim: Vertebrates acquired dim-light vision when an ancestral cone evolved into the rod photoreceptor at an unknown stage preceding the last common ancestor of extant jawed vertebrates (~420 million years ago Ma).
source: Vertebrates acquired dim-light vision when an ancestral cone evolved into the rod photoreceptor at an unknown stage preceding the last common ancestor of extant jawed vertebrates (∼420 million years ago Ma).
evidence: This claim is supported by references to established scientific knowledge about vertebrate evolution and the timing of the last common ancestor of jawed vertebrates.

claim: The lamprey line diverged ~505 Ma.
source: as their line diverged ∼505 Ma and later displayed high-morphological stability
evidence: This timing is cited from the literature (Erwin et al., 2011) as indicated in the Introduction section.

claim: Lamprey short photoreceptors (SPs) exhibit efficient amplification of the effect of single photons.
source: Several key functional features of jawed vertebrate rods are present in their phylogenetically homologous photoreceptors in lamprey: crucially, the efficient amplification of the effect of single photons, measured by multiple parameters
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental measurements of single photon responses presented in the Results section and Figure 5.

claim: Rod signals flow into cones in lamprey photoreceptors.
source: and the flow of rod signals into cones
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing that SPs feed their signals to LPs, as shown in Figure 1C-F and described in the Results.

claim: The functional similarities between lamprey SPs and jawed vertebrate rods make convergent evolution unlikely.
source: These results make convergent evolution in the jawless and jawed vertebrate lines unlikely
evidence: This is an inference based on the multiple functional similarities observed between lamprey SPs and jawed vertebrate rods.

claim: Rods originated early in vertebrate evolution, implying strong selective pressure toward dim-light vision in Cambrian ecosystems.
source: and indicate an early origin of rods, implying strong selective pressure toward dim-light vision in Cambrian ecosystems
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the functional data on lamprey photoreceptors combined with phylogenetic timing.

claim: By the middle Cambrian, camera-type eyes were already present in stem vertebrates.
source: The fossil record shows that by the middle Cambrian, camera-type eyes were already present in stem vertebrates (Morris and Caron, 2014)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to fossil record evidence.

claim: Spatially resolved vision provided a major competitive advantage in Cambrian biota.
source: supporting the emerging concept that spatially resolved vision provided a major competitive advantage in those biota (Paterson et al., 2011)
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Lampreys are the only surviving jawless vertebrates together with hagfish.
source: Lampreys, the only surviving jawless vertebrates together with the related hagfish (Heimberg et al., 2010)
evidence: This is established knowledge in vertebrate taxonomy, supported by citation.

claim: The lamprey line diverged during the Cambrian (~505 Ma).
source: In fact, their line diverged during the Cambrian (∼505 Ma [Erwin et al., 2011])
evidence: This timing is supported by citation to Erwin et al., 2011.

claim: Lampreys remained remarkably stable in their external morphology after divergence.
source: and they later remained remarkably stable. This is true both of their external morphology, as revealed by fossil specimens (Janvier and Arsenault, 2002; Gess et al., 2006; Janvier et al., 2006; Chang et al., 2014)
evidence: This is supported by citations to fossil evidence.

claim: Lampreys possess primeval features such as the absence of bilateral limbs and myelinated axons.
source: as demonstrated by primeval features such as the absence of bilateral limbs and of myelinated axons
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge about lampreys.

claim: Lampreys possess the simplest nervous system among vertebrates.
source: and by their possession of the simplest nervous system among vertebrates
evidence: This is established knowledge in comparative neurobiology.

claim: Adult lampreys have camera-type eyes with layered retinas containing all the major neuronal classes present in jawed vertebrates.
source: Adult lampreys have camera-type eyes with layered retinas containing all the major neuronal classes present in jawed vertebrates (Lamb, 2013)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Lamb, 2013.

claim: Lamprey retinas send retinotopically organized projections to the tectum.
source: and sending retinotopically organized projections to the tectum (Jones et al., 2009)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Jones et al., 2009.

claim: Lampreys have a photosensory pineal organ.
source: as well as a photosensory pineal organ (Pu and Dowling, 1981)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Pu and Dowling, 1981.

claim: Current molecular genetic evidence indicates that modern rods evolved from an ancestral cone.
source: Current molecular genetic evidence indicates that modern rods evolved from an ancestral cone (Okano et al., 1992; Yokoyama, 2000; Lamb et al., 2007; Kawamura and Tachibanaki, 2008; Shichida and Matsuyama, 2009)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to molecular genetic studies.

claim: Vision in near darkness is a relatively recent acquisition in vertebrates.
source: implying that vision in near darkness is a relatively recent acquisition (Lamb, 2013)
evidence: This is an inference from molecular genetic evidence, supported by citation.

claim: Rod evolutionary emergence occurred after the appearance of the precursor of rhodopsin and other rod-specific phototransduction protein isoforms.
source: This advance must have occurred (i) after the appearance of the precursor of rhodopsin and of other rod-specific phototransduction proteins isoforms
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the molecular requirements for rod function.

claim: Rod evolutionary emergence occurred before the initial diversification of extant jawed vertebrates (~420 Ma).
source: and (ii) before the initial diversification of extant jawed vertebrates (∼420 Ma; Erwin et al., 2011) endowed with modern rods
evidence: This is supported by citation and knowledge of jawed vertebrate evolution.

claim: The sea squirt Ciona intestinalis has only one jawed vertebrate-related visual opsin.
source: the sea squirt Ciona intestinalis has only one jawed vertebrate-related visual opsin (Kusakabe et al., 2001)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kusakabe et al., 2001.

claim: Some lamprey species have all five major classes of visual opsins.
source: while some lamprey species have all five major classes (Yokoyama, 2000)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Yokoyama, 2000.

claim: Lamprey species have an Rh1 rhodopsin ortholog.
source: including an Rh1 rhodopsin ortholog (Pisani et al., 2006)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Pisani et al., 2006.

claim: The five opsin classes and rod-specific molecular toolbox emerged in the context of two rounds of whole-genome duplication called '2R'.
source: Recently, strong evidence has emerged indicating that these five opsin classes (and the rod-specific molecular toolbox) emerged in the context of two rounds of whole-genome duplication called '2R' (Kuraku et al., 2009; Lagman et al., 2013)
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent genomic studies.

claim: The lamprey line diverged from the main vertebrate line shortly after 2R.
source: Furthermore, analysis of the whole sea lamprey genome suggests that the lamprey line diverged from the main vertebrate line shortly after 2R (Smith et al., 2013)
evidence: This is supported by citation to genome analysis.

claim: Northern hemisphere lampreys have two types of photoreceptors with light-absorbing outer segments arranged in adjacent tiers.
source: The two types of photoreceptors in the retina of Northern hemisphere lampreys have light-absorbing outer segments arranged in adjacent tiers (Figure 1A): those of short photoreceptors (SPs) lie in an inner tier, while those of long photoreceptors (LPs) lie in an outer tier, next to the pigment epithelium.
evidence: This is supported by the image in Figure 1A showing the layered organization.

claim: Short photoreceptors (SPs) express an Rh1 rhodopsin ortholog.
source: Importantly, SPs express an Rh1 rhodopsin ortholog (Pisani et al., 2006)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Pisani et al., 2006.

claim: Some phototransduction protein isoforms of SPs clade with those of rods.
source: and some of their phototransduction protein isoforms examined thus far clade with those of rods (Muradov et al., 2008)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Muradov et al., 2008.

claim: SP outer segment discs appear continuous with the plasma membrane.
source: but they also have molecular and morphological features of cones including outer segment discs that appear continuous with the plasma membrane (Dickson and Graves, 1979)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Dickson and Graves, 1979.

claim: SPs are homologues of jawed vertebrate rods.
source: Thus, while they retain archaic features of a cone progenitor, SPs are homologues of jawed vertebrate rods (Lamb, 2013)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Lamb, 2013 and is an inference from molecular and morphological data.

claim: LPs express an LWS red cone opsin.
source: LPs, on the other hand, express an LWS red cone opsin
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about LP molecular characteristics.

claim: LPs have a molecular fingerprint consistent with cones.
source: and have a molecular fingerprint consistent with cones (Muradov et al., 2008)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Muradov et al., 2008.

claim: The dark membrane potential of SPs is −43.2 ± 0.7 mV (n = 30).
source: First, we made perforated patch-clamp recordings from photoreceptor inner segments and found that the dark membrane potential was of −43.2 ± 0.7 mV for SPs (n = 30)
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data from patch-clamp recordings.

claim: The dark membrane potential of LPs is −45.9 ± 1.1 mV (n = 10).
source: and −45.9 ± 1.1 mV for LPs (n = 10)
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data from patch-clamp recordings.

claim: The dark membrane potentials of lamprey photoreceptors are in line with those of jawed vertebrate rods and cones.
source: these values are in line with those of jawed vertebrate rods and cones (Cangiano et al., 2012)
evidence: This is a comparison to literature values, supported by citation.

claim: Input resistances of SPs are 518 ± 41 MΩ (n = 8).
source: Input resistances were 518 ± 41 MΩ (n = 8; SPs)
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data.

claim: Input resistances of LPs are 442 ± 68 MΩ (n = 9).
source: and 442 ± 68 MΩ (n = 9; LPs)
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data.

claim: The membrane time constant of SPs is 31.9 ± 4.9 ms (n = 8).
source: The membrane time constants, obtained by fitting single exponentials to the early rise of a current step response, were 31.9 ± 4.9 ms (n = 8; SPs)
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data.

claim: The membrane time constant of LPs is 12.9 ± 1.3 ms (n = 9).
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data with statistical significance.

claim: The electrical properties of SP inner segments seem adapted to process slower photocurrent changes than those of LPs.
source: Thus, the electrical properties of the inner segments of SPs seem adapted to process slower photocurrent changes than those of LPs.
evidence: This is an inference from the measured membrane time constants.

claim: Both SPs and LPs express the hyperpolarization-activated current Ih.
source: Both SPs (n = 7) and LPs (n = 2) expressed the hyperpolarization-activated current Ih, similarly to rods and cones (Della Santina et al., 2012)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and citation to similar findings in rods and cones.

claim: Ih current in lamprey photoreceptors is abolished by ZD7288 (100 µM).
source: Ih was abolished by ZD7288 (100 µM, n = 1 SP; Figure 1B)
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Light stimulation evokes hyperpolarization in both SPs and LPs.
source: Light stimulation evoked a hyperpolarization in both photoreceptors (Figure 1C,D)
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figures 1C and 1D.

claim: SPs show peak membrane potential changes of up to 30 mV in response to saturating flashes.
source: with peak changes in membrane potential of up to 30 mV (SPs)
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data.

claim: LPs show peak membrane potential changes of up to 32 mV in response to saturating flashes.
source: and 32 mV (LPs) in response to saturating flashes
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data.

claim: The ratio of sensitivities of SPs at 520 nm and 590 nm is 4.4 ± 0.9 (n = 5).
source: From the curves, we obtained a ratio of 4.4 ± 0.9 (n = 5) for the sensitivities of these photoreceptors at 520 nm and 590 nm.
evidence: This is calculated from experimental data.

claim: The sensitivity ratio of SPs at 520/590 nm is in reasonably good agreement with the ratio of 5.6 predicted by an 11A1 visual pigment template with λmax of 517 nm.
source: This value is in reasonably good agreement with the ratio of 5.6 predicted by an 11A1 visual pigment template (Govardovskii et al., 2000) having a λmax of 517 nm (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: This is a comparison between experimental data and theoretical prediction based on known pigment properties.

claim: The absorbance maximum of SP outer segments is 517 nm.
source: the absorbance maximum of SP outer segments found with microspectrophotometry (Govardovskii and Lychakov, 1984)
evidence: This is supported by citation to microspectrophotometry data.

claim: LP flash responses display two components.
source: For LPs, the flash responses displayed two components (Figure 1D,F)
evidence: This is observed in experimental data shown in Figures 1D and 1F.

claim: The first component of LP flash responses has kinetics, sensitivity, and spectral preference similar to SPs.
source: the first component had kinetics, sensitivity, and spectral preference similar to SPs
evidence: This is an observation from experimental data comparing LP and SP responses.

claim: The second component of LP flash responses has faster kinetics and lower sensitivity than the first component.
source: the second component had faster kinetics, lower sensitivity
evidence: This is an observation from experimental data.

claim: The ratio of sensitivities at 520 nm and 590 nm for the second component of LP responses is 1.1 ± 0.04 (n = 6).
source: and a ratio of sensitivities at 520 nm and 590 nm of 1.1 ± 0.04 (n = 6)
evidence: This is calculated from experimental data.

claim: The sensitivity ratio of 1.1 for the second LP component agrees with the value predicted by an 11A1 template with λmax at 555 nm.
source: This ratio agrees with the value of 1.1 predicted by an 11A1 template (Govardovskii et al., 2000), whose λmax is set at 555 nm (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: This is a comparison between experimental data and theoretical prediction.

claim: The absorbance maximum of LP outer segments is 555 nm.
source: the absorbance maximum of LP outer segments (Govardovskii and Lychakov, 1984)
evidence: This is supported by citation to microspectrophotometry data.

claim: The first component of LP flash responses represents input from SPs, probably mediated by gap junctions.
source: It is likely that the first component of the flash response from LPs represents input from SPs, probably mediated by gap junctions
evidence: This is an inference from the similarity of the first LP component to SP responses.

claim: Rod-cone coupling via gap junctions exists in jawed vertebrates.
source: this arrangement would represent in lamprey retina an arrangement homologous to rod-cone coupling in jawed vertebrates (Asteriti et al., 2014)
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Thin telodendria emanate from the synaptic pole of lamprey photoreceptors and extend laterally into the inner plexiform layer.
source: In support of this interpretation, we observed with Lucifer Yellow injection thin telodendria emanating from the synaptic pole of the photoreceptors and extending laterally into the inner plexiform layer (Figure 2)
evidence: This is experimental observation shown in Figure 2.

claim: The only known function of telodendrial processes in jawed vertebrates is forming inter-photoreceptor junctional contacts.
source: the only known function of these processes in jawed vertebrates is that of forming inter-photoreceptor junctional contacts (O'Brien et al., 2012)
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Some visual pigment molecules in SP outer segments were bleached in control conditions.
source: Thus, some of the visual pigment molecules in SP outer segments were indeed bleached.
evidence: This is inferred from the increase in sensitivity after 9-cis-Retinal treatment.

claim: The sensitivity at 520 nm of two SPs increased by 2.0 and 2.5-fold after superfusion with 9-cis-Retinal.
source: The sensitivity at 520 nm of two SPs, recorded both in control and during delivery of 9-cis-Retinal, increased by 2.0 and 2.5-fold (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Sensitivity was higher in regenerated than in control SPs (p < 0.01).
source: Moreover, sensitivity was higher (p < 0.01) in regenerated than in control SPs: half-maximal response at 520 nm evoked with flashes (i1/2) of 63 ± 11 photons·µm−2 (n = 12; regenerated) vs 149 ± 25 photons·µm−2 (n = 10; control).
evidence: This is experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: The ratio of sensitivities at 520 and 590 nm did not differ significantly between regenerated and control SPs (p = 0.42).
source: The ratio of sensitivities at 520 and 590 nm did not differ significantly (p = 0.42) between regenerated and control SPs: 5.6 ± 1.0 (n = 5; regenerated) vs 4.4 ± 0.9 (n = 5; control).
evidence: This is experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: Integration time increased by 2.6-fold in one SP after superfusion with 9-cis-Retinal.
source: In one SP, integration time increased by 2.6-fold after superfusion with 9-cis-Retinal
evidence: This is experimental data from a single cell.

claim: Integration time was significantly higher in regenerated than in control SPs (p < 0.001).
source: and the same parameter was significantly higher (p < 0.001) in regenerated than in control SPs (Figure 3B): 0.81 ± 0.14 s (n = 9; regenerated) vs 0.32 ± 0.05 s (n = 13; control).
evidence: This is experimental data with statistical analysis, shown in Figure 3B.

claim: SPs were in a state of bleaching desensitization.
source: These results strongly suggest that SPs were in a state of bleaching desensitization.
evidence: This is inferred from the increase in sensitivity and integration time after pigment regeneration.

claim: The sensitivity at 520 nm of one LP increased by 22-fold after superfusion with 9-cis-Retinal.
source: In one LP, the sensitivity at 520 nm increased by 22-fold after superfusion with 9-cis-Retinal (Figure 3C; second, lower sensitivity component).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Sensitivity was much higher in regenerated than in control LPs (p < 0.05).
source: Moreover, sensitivity was much higher (p < 0.05) in regenerated than in control LPs: half-maximal response at 520 nm evoked with flashes (i1/2) of 2385 ± 513 photons·µm−2 (n = 7; regenerated) vs 1.9 × 105 ± 1.1 × 105 photons·µm−2 (n = 7; control; second, lower sensitivity component
evidence: This is experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: The ratio of sensitivities at 520 and 590 nm went from 1.1 to 1.7 in one LP treated with 9-cis-Retinal.
source: Specifically, the ratio of sensitivities at 520 and 590 nm went from 1.1 to 1.7 in the single LP treated with 9-cis-Retinal (Figure 3C, compare large and small circles)
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The ratio of sensitivities at 520 and 590 nm was significantly higher in regenerated than in control LPs (p < 0.01).
source: and was significantly higher (p < 0.01) in regenerated than in control LPs: 1.8 ± 0.1 (n = 7; regenerated) vs 1.1 ± 0.04 (n = 6; control).
evidence: This is experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: After pigment regeneration, the photovoltage responses of SPs remained markedly slower than those of LPs.
source: After pigment regeneration, the photovoltage responses of SPs, recorded with patch clamp, remained markedly slower than those of LPs (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: This is experimental observation shown in Figures 4A and 4B.

claim: For regenerated SPs, the TTP at i1/2 was 0.29 ± 0.04 s (n = 11).
source: for SPs, the TTP was 0.29 ± 0.04 s (n = 11)
evidence: This is experimental data from linear fits.

claim: For regenerated SPs, the τrec at i1/2 was 1.05 ± 0.27 s (n = 11).
source: and the τrec was 1.05 ± 0.27 s (n = 11)
evidence: This is experimental data from linear fits.

claim: For regenerated LPs, the TTP at i1/2 was 0.11 ± 0.007 s (n = 10; p < 0.001).
source: In contrast, for LPs, the TTP was only 0.11 ± 0.007 s (n = 10; p < 0.001)
evidence: This is experimental data from linear fits with statistical significance.

claim: For regenerated LPs, the τrec at i1/2 was 0.12 ± 0.02 (n = 10; p < 0.001).
source: and the τrec only 0.12 ± 0.02 (n = 10; p < 0.001)
evidence: This is experimental data from linear fits with statistical significance.

claim: When compared at flash strengths eliciting responses of similar fractional amplitude, SPs were slower than LPs.
source: Therefore, when compared at flash strengths eliciting responses of similar fractional amplitude, SPs were indeed slower than LPs.
evidence: This is an inference from the TTP and τrec measurements.

claim: The corrected i1/2 of regenerated SPs at λmax was 63 ± 11 photons·µm−2 (n = 12).
source: This implied that our 520-nm flashes essentially coincided with λmax (517 nm, see above) and that no correction was necessary for their i1/2 of 63 ± 11 photons·µm−2 (n = 12).
evidence: This is experimental data with reasoning about spectral corrections.

claim: The corrected i1/2 of regenerated LPs at λmax was 777 ± 167 photons·µm−2 (n = 7).
source: Taking into account the off-peak position of our flashes (520 nm) relative to the λmax of this action spectrum (541 nm) and the smaller quantum efficiency of regenerated pigment, the corrected i1/2 of LPs was 777 ± 167 photons·µm−2 (n = 7).
evidence: This is experimental data with corrections for spectral position and quantum efficiency.

claim: The i1/2 of LPs was much higher than that of SPs (p < 0.001).
source: The i1/2 of LPs was much higher than that of SPs (p < 0.001).
evidence: This is a statistical comparison of experimental data.

claim: Regenerated SPs had absolute dim-flash sensitivity of 0.61 ± 0.17 mV·photons−1·µm2 (n = 8).
source: Regenerated SPs were highly sensitive, with absolute and fractional dim-flash sensitivities in patch clamp of 0.61 ± 0.17 mV·photons−1·µm2 (n = 8)
evidence: This is experimental data from patch-clamp recordings.

claim: Regenerated SPs had fractional dim-flash sensitivity of 3.0 ± 0.6%·photons−1·µm2 (n = 8).
source: and 3.0 ± 0.6%·photons−1·µm2 (n = 8)
evidence: This is experimental data from patch-clamp recordings.

claim: The fractional single photon response of SPs estimated from patch clamp was 2.6 ± 0.5%·R*−1 (n = 8).
source: We obtained a first estimate of their fractional single photon response of 2.6 ± 0.5%·R* −1 (n = 8) by dividing the fractional dim-flash sensitivity with a theoretical effective collecting area of 1.18 µm2·R*·photons−1
evidence: This is calculated from experimental data using theoretical collecting area.

claim: The absolute amplitude of the single photon response (a) in SPs was 0.41 ± 0.04 pA (n = 10).
source: We estimated the absolute amplitude of the single photon response (a) to be 0.41 ± 0.04 pA (n = 10), by dividing the increase in the time-dependent variance by the mean response for each SP (Figure 5B) (Rieke and Baylor, 1998)
evidence: This is experimental data from suction electrode recordings analyzed with variance methods, shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The fractional amplitude of the single photon response (a%) in SPs was 2.6 ± 0.3%·R*−1 (n = 10).
source: The fractional amplitude of the single photon response (a%), determined for each SP on the basis of its maximal response to a single saturating flash delivered prior to the dim flash trains, was 2.6 ± 0.3%·R* −1 (n = 10)
evidence: This is experimental data from suction electrode recordings.

claim: The signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) in SPs was 1.5 ± 0.1 (n = 10).
source: Lastly, the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), determined for each SP as the ratio of a over the standard deviation of the biological component of dark noise measured between consecutive dim flashes (0.5–20 Hz), was 1.5 ± 0.1 (n = 10).
evidence: This is experimental data from suction electrode recordings.

claim: The values of a, a%, and SNR in SPs are within the range reported for jawed vertebrate rods.
source: Importantly, the values of a, a%, and SNR in SPs are within the range reported for jawed vertebrate rods (Figure 6).
evidence: This is a comparison of experimental data to literature values, shown in Figure 6.

claim: Dark currents measured with patch clamp in SPs were 13 ± 3 pA (n = 4).
source: observed similar dark currents (maximum current change with a saturating flash) with patch clamp (13 ± 3 pA, n = 4)
evidence: This is experimental data from patch-clamp recordings.

claim: Dark currents measured with suction electrodes in SPs were 16 ± 1 pA (n = 10).
source: and suction electrodes (16 ± 1 pA, n = 10)
evidence: This is experimental data from suction electrode recordings.

claim: The collecting area of SPs measured with suction electrodes was 0.83 ± 0.17 µm2·R*·photons−1 (n = 10).
source: and (iii) measured similar collecting areas (0.83 ± 0.17 µm2·R*·photons−1, n = 10; ratio of the squared mean response over the product of the variance increase and the flash strength [Rieke and Baylor, 1998]) to theoretical prediction (1.18 µm2·R*·photons−1).
evidence: This is experimental data from suction electrode recordings compared to theoretical prediction.

claim: The amplification constant of phototransduction in lamprey SPs was 0.59 ± 0.09 s−2 at 9–11°C (n = 10).
source: The single photon response analysis made with suction pipettes allowed us to estimate an amplification constant of phototransduction (Pugh and Lamb, 1993) in lamprey SPs of 0.59 ± 0.09 s−2 at 9–11°C (n = 10)
evidence: This is experimental data from suction electrode recordings.

claim: The amplification constant of lamprey SPs lies between that of large amphibian rods at room temperature (~0.1 s−2) and that of small mammalian rods at body temperature (~8 s−2).
source: which lies between that of the large amphibian rods at room temperature (∼0.1 s−2) and that of small mammalian rods at body temperature (∼8 s−2) (Lamb and Pugh, 2006)
evidence: This is a comparison of experimental data to literature values.

claim: The integration time measured with suction electrodes in SPs was 1.45 ± 0.10 s (n = 10).
source: The integration time measured with suction electrodes was 1.45 ± 0.10 s (n = 10)
evidence: This is experimental data from suction electrode recordings.

claim: The high-amplification constant and relatively long integration time are key contributors to SPs' single photon performance.
source: Taken together, the high-amplification constant and relatively long integration time are key contributors to SPs' single photon performance.
evidence: This is an inference from the measured amplification constant and integration time.

claim: Dark membrane potentials of around −45 mV, hyperpolarizing responses of up to 30 mV upon illumination, and expression of Ih current are typical traits of jawed vertebrate photoreceptors.
source: dark membrane potentials of around −45 mV, hyperpolarizing responses of up to 30 mV upon illumination, and the expression of a prominent hyperpolarization-activated Ih current are all typical traits of jawed vertebrate photoreceptors
evidence: This is established knowledge about jawed vertebrate photoreceptors.

claim: These general properties of lamprey photoreceptors must have been in place by the middle Cambrian.
source: and must therefore have been in place already by the middle Cambrian
evidence: This is an inference from the similarity of lamprey and jawed vertebrate photoreceptor properties combined with phylogenetic timing.

claim: Bleaching adaptation is present in lamprey SPs.
source: A similar conclusion can be made for bleaching adaptation, which we confirmed to be present in SPs.
evidence: This is confirmed by experimental data showing sensitivity changes after pigment regeneration.

claim: In jawed vertebrates, bleaching adaptation results from very low-constitutive activity of free opsin and occurs in both rods and cones exposed to bleaching lights.
source: In jawed vertebrates, this phenomenon is the result of a very low-constitutive activity of free opsin and occurs in both rods and cones exposed to bleaching lights (Cornwall and Fain, 1994; Cornwall et al., 1995; Fain et al., 2001; Lamb and Pugh, 2004).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: SPs are exquisitely sensitive to light.
source: We find that SPs are exquisitely sensitive to light
evidence: This is supported by experimental measurements of sensitivity.

claim: SPs feed their signals to the less sensitive but intrinsically faster LPs.
source: and feed their signals to the less sensitive but intrinsically faster LPs
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing the two-component response in LPs.

claim: Rods feed their signals to cones via gap junctions in jawed vertebrates.
source: similarly to the way rods feed their signals to cones via gap junctions in jawed vertebrates (Asteriti et al., 2014)
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Telodendria are ubiquitous in jawed vertebrates.
source: Telodendria are ubiquitous in jawed vertebrates
evidence: This is established knowledge about photoreceptor anatomy.

claim: In mammals, telodendrial processes extend only from cone pedicles.
source: While in mammals these processes are known to extend only from cone pedicles
evidence: This is established knowledge about mammalian photoreceptor anatomy.

claim: In cold-blooded vertebrates, telodendria are also formed by rods.
source: in cold-blooded vertebrates they are also formed by rods (Fadool, 2003)
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Rod-cone coupling is thought to provide a secondary route for rod signals when the high-gain output synapse of rods is saturated.
source: Since rod-cone coupling is thought to provide a secondary route for rod signals when the high-gain output synapse of rods is saturated (Attwell et al., 1987)
evidence: This is a hypothesis from the literature supported by citation.

claim: In mammalian photoreceptors, the Ih current has been proposed to assist rod-cone signaling via gap junctions.
source: Furthermore, in mammalian photoreceptors, the Ih current has been proposed to assist rod-cone signaling via gap junctions (Seeliger et al., 2011)
evidence: This is a hypothesis from the literature supported by citation.

claim: The Ih current could play a role in rod-cone signaling in the lamprey retina.
source: a role it could also play in the lamprey retina given the presence of telodendria and SP–LP signal flow
evidence: This is speculation based on the presence of Ih current and anatomical features in lamprey.

claim: Dark-adapted SPs approach the efficiency of jawed vertebrate rods in terms of absolute and fractional single photon response and SNR.
source: With regards to scotopic performance, we found that dark-adapted SPs approach the efficiency of jawed vertebrate rods, both in terms of absolute and fractional single photon response and of its SNR.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data compared to literature values.

claim: Our last common ancestor in the middle Cambrian had already evolved scotopic vision.
source: Taken together, our findings raise the strong possibility that our last common ancestor in the middle Cambrian had already evolved scotopic vision.
evidence: This is an inference from the functional similarities between lamprey SPs and jawed vertebrate rods.

claim: The lamprey line diverged soon after two rounds of whole-genome duplication in stem vertebrates (2R).
source: Recent evidence indicates that the lamprey line diverged soon after (Smith et al., 2013) the occurrence of two rounds of whole-genome duplication in stem vertebrates (2R) (Dehal and Boore, 2005; Putnam et al., 2008)
evidence: This is supported by citations to genomic studies.

claim: Two rounds of whole-genome duplication led to the diversification of the ancestral visual opsin and phototransduction protein repertoire.
source: which led to the diversification of the ancestral visual opsin and phototransduction protein repertoire (Lagman et al., 2013)
evidence: This is supported by citation to genomic analysis.

claim: Dim-light vision appears to have been acquired rapidly once a dedicated set of genes became available for specializing a type of cone into the rod.
source: Therefore, dim-light vision appears to have been acquired rapidly once a dedicated set of genes became available for specializing a type of cone into the rod (Okano et al., 1992; Yokoyama, 2000; Lamb et al., 2007; Kawamura and Tachibanaki, 2008; Shichida and Matsuyama, 2009).
evidence: This is an inference from the timing of genome duplication and the functional properties of lamprey photoreceptors, supported by citations.

claim: The similarities between SPs and rods are multiple and extend from phototransduction to downstream processing.
source: the similarities between SPs and rods are multiple and extend from phototransduction to downstream processing
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings presented in the study.

claim: The photoreceptors specialized for scotopic vision in lampreys and in jawed vertebrates derive from one and the same precursor.
source: the photoreceptors specialized for scotopic vision in lampreys and in jawed vertebrates derive from one and the same precursor (and not from different ancestral cones)
evidence: This is based on molecular phylogenetic evidence of homology.

claim: Some of the phototransduction protein isoforms examined in SPs clade with those of rods.
source: some of the phototransduction protein isoforms examined thus far in SPs clade with those of rods
evidence: This is supported by citation to Muradov et al., 2008.

claim: The newly evolved ability to operate in dim light would have provided a significant advantage to early vertebrates faced with intense competition in a rapidly evolving ecological landscape.
source: This newly evolved ability to operate in dim light would have provided a significant advantage to early vertebrates faced with intense competition in a rapidly evolving ecological landscape (Paterson et al., 2011; Lacalli, 2012).
evidence: This is speculation about evolutionary advantage supported by citations to ecological studies.

claim: A study on photoreceptors of a different lamprey species published in coincidence with the present work converges on the positive response to single photons.
source: In coincidence with the submission of the present work, a study on the photoreceptors of a different species of lamprey was published (Morshedian and Fain, 2015), based on suction electrode recordings from outer segments. Although our study examines a broader range of photoreceptor properties, with both patch-clamp and suction electrode recordings, the two studies converge on the positive response to single photons.
evidence: This is a comparison to a concurrent study supported by citation.
